chunks.text: Corpus of Seal Inscriptions of the Kassite Period Including Old Babylonian Forerunners

BM 130697, Courtesy of the Trustees of the British Museum    A comprehensive corpus of Kassite period seal inscriptions and related types. Director: Jon Taylor. Collaborators: Zsombor Földi, Enrique Jiménez, Ignacio Márquez-Rowe, Alexa Bartelmus.    The  Corpus of Seal Inscriptions of the Kassite period  (CSIK) gathers all known seal inscriptions from the Kassite period, together with related examples from the Late Old Babylonian, Middle Assyrian, and Middle Elamite periods. CSIK includes both cylinder seals themselves and ancient impressions preserved on clay. It updates and expands Limet’s classic  Les légendes des sceaux cassites  (1971). The number of texts known is now four times what is presented there.    The corpus has grown out of work by Taylor during preparation of the British Museum’s Catalogue of the Western Asiatic seals in the British Museum.  Cylinder seals 4: The Second Millennium BC Beyond Babylon  [https://www.britishmuseumshoponline.org/cylinder-seals-iv-the-second-millennium-bc.html]  (2016). This was supplemented by work conducted by Alexa Bartelmus during research towards her dissertation, now published as  Fragmente einer grossen Sprache: Sumerisch im Kontext der Schreiberausbildung des kassitenzeitlichen Babylonien  [https://www.degruyter.com/view/serial/468826]  (2016). Jiménez has contributed editions of the seals in the Yale Babylonian Collection. Földi has contributed editions of Old Babylonian “seal prayers”.    Basic statistics of the CSIK project:

Kassite-type seal inscriptions are unusually interesting. Previously, seal inscriptions had typically been short, naming the owner and giving limited information about them: the father’s name, and sometimes their profession or a line declaring that they are the servant of a particular deity or ruler. Kassite-type examples, by contrast, usually don’t mention the owner. In most cases where an owner is mentioned, it is simply as “the owner of this seal”. It is rare to find a specific name. When one is given, often it is that of a king or high official. The inscriptions typically take the form of a prayer for the well-being and longevity of their owner. When an inscription is present, it often dominates the seal. In some cases no space is given to iconography, or only filler motifs are present.   Kassite seal inscriptions can be difficult to read for several reasons. Firstly, the wording of the text is not standardised. Common elements can be shared, although usually in different combinations and orders. Secondly, the authors of the texts make use of unusual logograms. They exploit the sophistication of the writing system, not only using a variety of cuneiform signs for a given word, but also using a given sign to represent a variety of words. Thirdly, the quality of the carving of the signs sometimes seems to be low. Signs can have unfamiliar proportions, or unexpected wedge arrangements.   The language of the inscriptions in some cases appears to be Sumerian, in others Akkadian. Some that appear to be in Sumerian use Akkadian syntax. Every inscription in the corpus can be read satisfactorily in Akkadian.   Most seals can be dated only on the basis of their iconography. Where dates can be established, the Kassite corpus extends from the late 15th to the early 13th century BC.     18 Dec 2019
